extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, moral and political philosophy, and the theory of practical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating practical rules (arts, policies, moral precepts) that connects scientific theory to ends, handles exceptions, and grounds normative aims in teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of art are provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of conduct should be regarded as provisional: they are made for the most numerous or ordinary cases and therefore are always imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rules as default guidance when time or means do not permit a detailed analysis of the particular case; remain ready to modify or discard the rule when unusual circumstances obtain. Rules serve as admonitions about what is usually least perilous, not as absolute prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant reference of rules to scientific laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In complicated affairs (especially of states and societies), rules cannot be reliably followed without constantly referring back to the scientific laws on which they are founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know which contingencies modify or except a rule requires understanding the theoretical grounds; practitioners should trace rules back to the scientific principles that justify them before applying them to complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope of rules to ordinary, apprehendable conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For convenience, rules must be formed from less than an ideally perfect theory because including every contingency would make them too cumbrous to be apprehended and remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting rules, include only those conditions which require attention in ordinary cases; ensure the rule is simple enough for ordinary capacities while noting that this simplicity implies imperfection and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate manual arts from complex social/political arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In manual arts, where requisite conditions are few and unmentioned conditions are observable or learned by practice, rules can often be safely followed by those knowing only the rule; in social and political affairs this is not so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the domain's complexity before deciding whether a rule may be applied without deeper knowledge: low-complexity domains permit rule-following by novices; high-complexity domains require theoretical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing practice solely from universal maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is erroneous to deduce conduct for particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims without constantly referring to speculative science and the possibility of conflicting ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt unbending, geometrical-style practical principles as ultimate premises; always examine whether following a given principle in a particular case will produce the intended effects or conflict with other desirable ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and justify the end as an act of Art (not Science)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the end (what is to be aimed at) belongs exclusively to Art; propositions prescribing what 'ought' to be are not scientific but normative and must be justified by general premises determining proper objects of approbation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating rules, explicitly state the end they aim at and provide normative justification (teleological or other) because science alone does not establish what ends ought to be pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule systems must include the speculative propositions that justify them
rubrics_metrics.description: An art consists of the rules together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose practical doctrines (arts) by pairing rules with the intermediate scientific truths and propositions necessary to show on what conditions the desired effects depend, so practitioners can assess applicability and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form intermediate scientific principles linking means and ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Between abstract science and concrete rules there should be intermediate scientific truths (general relations between available means and the end) constituting the scientific theory of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After identifying the end and surveying available resources and conditions, distill the fewest and most extensive propositions that express how means relate to the end; practical methods should follow as corollaries from these propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When feasible, prefer case-specific scientific inquiry to rule application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where circumstances permit, the scientific process of analyzing the particular case should be used to frame or modify a rule from the data of that case instead of relying solely on the common rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If time and means exist, undertake a detailed investigation to determine whether the common rule fits the particular situation; use rules mainly where detailed analysis is impractical or unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a single ultimate standard for judging conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness of ends; if multiple ultimate principles existed they could conflict, so some one standard is needed as umpire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coherence among rules by making them consistent with a single, clearly stated ultimate principle of conduct to avoid irreconcilable approvals and condemnations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduciveness to happiness as the test of rules (teleological standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform, and the test by which they should be tried, is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind (or of all sentient beings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the promotion of happiness as the justificatory standard for ends and for adjudicating between conflicting rules; recognize this is a justificatory controller rather than an injunction that every act aim solely at immediate happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow higher ends (character cultivation) but justify them teleologically
rubrics_metrics.description: Some virtuous actions or modes of action may sacrifice immediate happiness, but they can be justified only if, on the whole, they conduce to more happiness (for example, by cultivating dispositions that ultimately increase幸福).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When endorsing rules that promote ideals or character at the expense of short-term happiness, provide argument showing how such cultivation produces greater aggregate happiness or other teleological benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientists must not usurp the role of deciding ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific observer's role is to show causal relations and effective means; it is not the business of science, merely as such, to decide what ends ought to be pursued—those require teleological justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scientific findings are used in policy or moral recommendation, separate factual causal claims from normative claims and supply proper normative premises before prescribing actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules should state their ordinary applicability and likely exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common rules may properly serve as an admonition about what is usually well adapted, but if unsuitable to the case at hand, the reason will likely be some unusual circumstance; practitioners should indicate such exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating rules, specify the ordinary conditions under which they apply and flag the kinds of unusual circumstances that should prompt deviation or reanalysis.
